article_content: India is considering reducing import taxes on select electric vehicles from the UK to help finalize a free-trade agreement between the two nations by the end of the year, according to people familiar with the discussions. New Delhi may offer a tariff of 30% on up to 2,500 UK-made electric vehicles annually, each priced over $80,000. Currently, India levies taxes ranging from 70% to 100% on imported, fully built vehicles, depending on their value. Import concessions for electric vehicles are among the few outstanding issues in UK-India free trade negotiations. Prime Ministers Rishi Sunak (UK) and Narendra Modi (India) had hoped to finalize the deal last month, but it is now expected to be announced closer to December, according to Bloomberg News. Officials from India’s trade ministry and the UK’s trade department have declined to comment, as discussions are ongoing. As the world’s most populous country, India is seeing growing interest in electric vehicles, particularly among middle-class and affluent buyers. However, the uptake has been slow due to high prices, limited model choices, and inadequate charging infrastructure. Opening the EV market could accelerate cleaner transportation in a nation facing severe air pollution. Last year, electric vehicle sales in India totalled 49,800 units, accounting for just 1.3% of 3.8 million passenger vehicles sold (BloombergNEF). Tata Motors’ Nexon.ev, the country’s best-selling EV, is priced under 1.5 million rupees ($18,000). German luxury brands like BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Audi sell electric cars in India priced over $80,000. India’s government remains cautious about EV imports and is focused on encouraging domestic manufacturing, having introduced a $3.1 billion production-linked incentive program for local EV production in 2021. No final decision has been made yet about adjusting EV import tariffs. Some progress has already been made on related trade issues, including lowering tariffs on British cars and Scotch whisky. The UK-India free-trade deal could potentially double bilateral trade by 2030 through reduced tariffs and improved market access. It is considered politically significant: a potential Brexit win for the UK and a boost for India’s manufacturing goals. For unassembled imported cars, India’s import duty ranges from 15% to 35%. India also recently became the most represented country in the QS World University Rankings: Asia 2024, overtaking China, reflecting advances in its higher education system. Stay updated with business and market news through The Economic Times News App.

Nuova Delhi potrebbe offrire una tariffa del 30% su un massimo di 2.500 veicoli elettrici britannici all'anno, ciascuno con un prezzo superiore agli 80.000 dollari. Attualmente, l'India applica tasse comprese tra il 70% e il 100% sui veicoli completamente assemblati importati, in base al loro valore. article_content: American striker Clint Dempsey says the U.S. team has gained confidence from strong performances against Brazil, Spain, and England, but he emphasizes that Friday's World Cup match against Slovenia is a must-not-lose for his side. Dempsey scored the fortunate goal that slipped through England goalkeeper Robert Green's hands, securing a 1-1 draw in the U.S.'s opening World Cup game last Saturday in South Africa. The Americans performed well to avoid defeat against one of the tournament favorites, and Dempsey credits the experience of reaching last year's Confederations Cup final with giving the team the belief to compete with top sides. The U.S. defeated European champions Spain 2-0 in the semifinals of that tournament and led Brazil by two goals in the final before eventually losing 3-2. Before facing England, Dempsey told CNN, 'We knew that if we played our best, we could get a result, just like we did at the Confederations Cup against the top teams.' Midfielder Michael Bradley echoed these sentiments, describing the team as 'battle-hardened.' 'We've had three or four years of playing the best teams in the world. When we face a team like England, there's a sense of experience. We know what to expect and what we need to do,' Bradley said to CNN. 'That mentality will take us where we want to go.' With the top two teams from the group advancing to the knockout stages, the U.S. and England are considered favorites to progress ahead of Slovenia and Algeria. However, since Slovenia beat Algeria in their opening match, Dempsey emphasized that the U.S. cannot afford to falter against the smallest nation to qualify for the finals. 'If we lose this game, we could be out of the tournament, so we have to make sure we take calculated risks going forward,' Dempsey said. 'We can't just attack recklessly and risk getting caught on the counter-attack.' Bradley, the son of U.S. coach Bob Bradley, said the American players would approach Slovenia with the same respect as England. 'The terms favorites or underdogs are labels others use, not us,' Bradley stated. 'We had respect for England and we have a lot of respect for Slovenia, knowing that will also be a challenging match.'

Dempsey ha segnato il gol fortunato che è passato tra le mani del portiere inglese Robert Green, assicurando un pareggio per 1-1 nella partita d'esordio della squadra statunitense ai Mondiali, sabato scorso in Sudafrica. Gli americani hanno giocato bene per evitare la sconfitta contro una delle squadre favorite del torneo e Dempsey attribuisce all'esperienza di aver raggiunto la finale della Confederations Cup dello scorso anno il fatto di aver dato al gruppo la convinzione di potersela giocare con le migliori. Gli Stati Uniti hanno battuto i campioni europei della Spagna 2-0 in semifinale e sono stati in vantaggio di due gol contro il Brasile in finale, prima di subire una rimonta e perdere 3-2. Prima della partita contro l'Inghilterra, Dempsey ha detto alla CNN: 'Sapevamo che giocando al meglio potevamo ottenere un risultato, proprio come abbiamo fatto alla Confederations Cup contro le grandi squadre.' Il centrocampista Michael Bradley ha confermato queste sensazioni, descrivendo la squadra come 'forgiata in battaglia'. 'Da tre o quattro anni giochiamo contro le migliori squadre al mondo. Quando affrontiamo squadre come l'Inghilterra, abbiamo quella esperienza. Sappiamo cosa aspettarci e cosa dobbiamo fare,' ha detto Bradley alla CNN. 'Questa mentalità ci porterà dove vogliamo arrivare.' Con le prime due squadre del girone che accederanno alla fase a eliminazione diretta, Stati Uniti e Inghilterra sono considerati i favoriti per il passaggio del turno rispetto a Slovenia e Algeria. Tuttavia, visto che la Slovenia ha battuto l'Algeria nella partita inaugurale, Dempsey ha sottolineato che gli Stati Uniti non possono permettersi di sbagliare contro la nazione più piccola qualificata ai Mondiali. 'Se perdiamo questa partita, potremmo essere eliminati dal torneo, quindi dobbiamo assumerci rischi calcolati in attacco,' ha detto Dempsey. 'Non possiamo attaccare tutti indiscriminatamente e rischiare di subire gol in contropiede.' 'Abbiamo rispettato l'Inghilterra e rispettiamo molto anche la Slovenia, sapendo che sarà comunque una sfida difficile.'

article_content: A well-respected family of general practitioners who dedicated their lives to caring for the people of a remote Scottish island are to be honored with a memorial, it was revealed today. Dr. Alexander Macleod, originally from the Isle of Lewis, together with his family, spent more than 70 years providing medical care on North Uist in the Outer Hebrides. At one point, Dr. Macleod had delivered most of the babies born on the island. From the time Dr. Macleod established his practice in 1932 until his retirement in 1974, he visited patients across North Uist on foot and horseback. After his retirement, his son, Dr. John Macleod, continued serving the community until 2000. Dr. Alexander Macleod’s wife, Julia, was also a GP and often stepped in for her husband when he traveled to Berneray, Baleshare, or other surrounding islands to visit patients. A commemorative plaque honoring the Macleod family's service will be placed on a hill on North Uist, to be unveiled by Dr. John Gillies, chairman of the Royal College of General Practitioners of Scotland, a native of North Uist and one of the many babies delivered by Dr. Alexander Macleod. During his years of practice, healthcare was extremely limited on the island, meaning Dr. Macleod frequently performed dental extractions and a wide range of medical procedures out of necessity. In recollections shared by Dr. John Macleod, surgeries were part of the family home, with the dining room doubling as the waiting room, and dental work was done on-site due to the infrequent visits of dentists. The Macleods have been compared to the fictional Dr. Finlay, created by A. J. Cronin, for their dedication to caring for their community throughout their patients' lives. Dr. Alexander Macleod was one of the first island doctors supported by the Highlands and Islands Medical Service, a pioneering initiative established in 1913 that transformed rural Scottish healthcare decades before the founding of the National Health Service. With few doctors over a vast area, the Macleods served with exceptional commitment, often providing 24-hour care, delivering children, and even organizing the first recorded air ambulance flight to the Western Isles in the 1930s. The family’s contributions are also recognized in the National Museum of Scotland’s exhibition, 'Scotland: A Changing Nation.' Their dedication and compassion are considered exemplary by their peers, including Dr. Gillies, who credits the Macleods as key influences and role models in general practice. The Macleods valued teamwork with district nurses, acknowledging them as an essential part of delivering healthcare to North Uist's isolated population.

Il dottor Alexander Macleod, originario dell'Isola di Lewis, insieme alla sua famiglia, ha fornito assistenza medica per oltre 70 anni a North Uist, nelle Ebridi Esterne. In un certo periodo, il dottor Macleod aveva fatto nascere la maggior parte dei bambini dell'isola. Dopo il suo ritiro, suo figlio, il dottor John Macleod, ha continuato a servire la comunità fino al 2000. La moglie del dottor Alexander Macleod, Julia, era anch'essa medico di famiglia e spesso lo sostituiva durante le sue visite a Berneray, Baleshare o in altre isole vicine. Una targa commemorativa che rende omaggio al servizio della famiglia Macleod sarà posata su una collina di North Uist e inaugurata dal dottor John Gillies, presidente del Royal College of General Practitioners of Scotland, originario di North Uist e uno dei tanti bambini nati grazie al dottor Alexander Macleod. Durante i suoi anni di servizio, l’assistenza sanitaria sull’isola era molto limitata, tanto che il dottor Macleod si trovava spesso a dover eseguire estrazioni dentarie e varie procedure mediche. Come ricordato dal dottor John Macleod, lo studio medico era parte della casa di famiglia, con la sala da pranzo che fungeva anche da sala d’attesa e le cure odontoiatriche avvenivano in casa per la rarità delle visite dei dentisti. I Macleod sono stati paragonati al personaggio di fantasia Dottor Finlay, creato da A.J. Cronin, per la loro dedizione totale alla salute della comunità. Il dottor Alexander Macleod fu tra i primi medici dell’isola sostenuti dall’Highlands and Islands Medical Service, un’iniziativa pionieristica avviata nel 1913 che rivoluzionò l’assistenza sanitaria nelle aree rurali scozzesi prima della nascita del Servizio Sanitario Nazionale. Con pochi medici e territori enormi da coprire, i Macleod mostrarono un impegno eccezionale: offrivano assistenza anche di notte, facevano nascere bambini e organizzarono addirittura il primo volo di ambulanza aerea registrato verso le Ebridi Occidentali negli anni Trenta. Il contributo della famiglia è riconosciuto anche nella mostra del National Museum of Scotland 'Scotland: A Changing Nation.' La loro dedizione e compassione sono considerate esemplari dai colleghi come il dottor Gillies, che indica i Macleod come modelli di riferimento nella medicina generale. I Macleod valorizzavano la collaborazione con le infermiere distrettuali, considerate fondamentali per l’assistenza della popolazione isolata di North Uist.

George Osborne has warned that Ed Miliband is bringing British politics back to a Cold War-era divide between the interventionist left and the free-market right. Speaking at the Institute of Directors annual conference at the Royal Albert Hall, the Chancellor suggested that the debate many believed was settled after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989—the superiority of free markets in promoting prosperity—has re-emerged. Osborne argued that, while figures like Tony Blair recognized the importance of free markets in funding public services, Miliband remains anchored in the past and could potentially harm businesses.

The Chancellor urged the business community to engage more actively in the ongoing political debate, emphasizing the need to advocate for policies that support enterprise, business, and a low-tax economy to ensure long-term prosperity. Osborne said, 'For the first time in my adult life, our future as a nation that supports business and free enterprise is up for debate. That debate seemed settled with the fall of the Berlin Wall.'

He further contrasted the current Labour leadership with previous ones, arguing that leaders like Tony Blair and David Cameron presented themselves as credible prime ministers, whereas Miliband does not. Osborne asserted that this dynamic provides Conservatives with a significant electoral advantage. He characterized Labour under Miliband as a party focused on past grievances instead of future solutions, and argued that the upcoming election will present a clear choice between forward-looking Conservative policies and what he describes as Labour's backward-looking agenda.

article_content: Big tech companies are frequently fined for violations such as price fixing, suppressing competition, and misusing data. However, it can take years for these companies to actually pay these penalties. Ireland's data regulator confirmed to AFP that Meta has not paid any of the ₹2 billion ($2.2 billion) in fines issued since last September. TikTok also reportedly owes hundreds of millions in unpaid fines. Amazon is still appealing a ₹746 million fine from 2021, according to Luxembourg's data regulator. Google continues to challenge over eight billion euros in EU fines for abusing its market position between 2017 and 2019. Apple has contested a ₹1.1 billion French antitrust fine and a demand to pay €13 billion in taxes to Ireland. This issue is global and affects tech companies of all sizes, not just the largest firms. This week, Australia confirmed that X (formerly Twitter) has not paid a fine for failing to explain its plans to address child sexual abuse content. X is now counter-suing. Critics argue that fining tech companies does little to deter misconduct, and urge stronger measures. Margarida Silva, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Multinationals in the Netherlands, noted that tech firms often pride themselves on being disruptive. 'Not paying fines fits with how we've seen big tech challenge enforcement,' she said. She contrasted this with the finance industry, where firms are incentivized to pay fines to reassure the public and investors. Romain Rard, a lawyer at Gide Loyrette Nouel in Paris, said it's standard for firms to appeal large fines, but they cannot simply ignore them. 'It’s not as if companies can just ignore the fine, challenge decisions, and hope to avoid payment,' he said. Some companies have succeeded in appeals—Intel and Qualcomm recently had substantial EU antitrust fines overturned or reduced. In other news: The Indian government is reviewing the legality of transferring unclaimed Sahara-Sebi Refund Account funds to the Consolidated Fund of India, with a provision to refund investors who stake claims later. Apple is targeting production of nearly ₹1 lakh crore worth of iPhones in India for the fiscal year ending March 2024, ramping up manufacturing capacity and already achieving over ₹60,000 crore in the first seven months. Meanwhile, Nawaz Modi, the estranged wife of Gautam Singhania, is seeking three-quarters of Singhania’s net worth (estimated at $1.4 billion) for herself and their two daughters as part of a family settlement.

Il garante irlandese per la protezione dei dati ha confermato all'AFP che Meta non ha pagato nessuna delle multe da ₹2 miliardi (2,2 miliardi di dollari) emesse dallo scorso settembre. Anche TikTok risulta dover pagare centinaia di milioni di multe non ancora saldate. Questo problema è globale e riguarda aziende tecnologiche di tutte le dimensioni, non solo le più grandi. Questa settimana, l’Australia ha confermato che X (ex Twitter) non ha pagato una multa per non aver illustrato i propri piani per contrastare i contenuti legati ad abusi sessuali su minori. Ha confrontato la situazione con il settore finanziario, dove le aziende sono incentivate a pagare le multe per rassicurare pubblici e investitori. Romain Rard, avvocato presso Gide Loyrette Nouel a Parigi, ha affermato che è normale presentare ricorso per grandi multe, ma non si possono semplicemente ignorare. Apple punta a produrre quasi ₹1 lakh crore di iPhone in India nell’anno fiscale che termina a marzo 2024, aumentando la capacità produttiva e avendo già superato i ₹60.000 crore nei primi sette mesi. article_content: Republicans are strongly opposing President Barack Obama's expected executive action, which may allow millions of undocumented workers to remain in the United States. Meanwhile, the immigration debate is exposing internal GOP divisions and raising questions about whether the party is following advice to reach out to Hispanic voters. Citing inaction by Congress, Obama said last Wednesday that he is done waiting for Republicans to negotiate a compromise on immigration. 'I promise you, the American people don't want me just standing around twiddling my thumbs,' he said. House Speaker John Boehner warned that any new executive moves would be 'a grievous mistake,' insisting that Congress must act on immigration in a step-by-step manner so the public can participate. Although Boehner acknowledged after the 2012 election that reform was needed, a bipartisan Senate bill failed in the Republican-led House, as many GOP representatives from secure districts were wary of primary challenges and chose not to advance reform. Recent actions by some Republicans seem to conflict with efforts to make the party more inclusive. As Congress remains gridlocked, Obama intends to proceed alone. Many GOP leaders and presidential hopefuls say a more welcoming message to Hispanic voters is crucial for the 2016 election, yet much of the party's rhetoric still appears unwelcoming to many Latinos. Before the August recess, the House passed a bill to prevent the President from renewing or granting deportation deferments to an estimated 600,000 young people brought to the U.S. illegally as children. If enacted, these individuals could face deportation. The vote was primarily along party lines, with some Republicans arguing the measure sent the wrong message. Carlos Gutierrez, a Republican and former Commerce Secretary, questioned his party's approach on CNN, asking, 'Why are Republicans continuing to shoot themselves in the foot?' Iowa Rep. Steve King, a main supporter of the House bill, was confronted at an event attended by Sen. Rand Paul. A woman worried about being deported if the bill became law questioned King. Paul, who has focused on expanding GOP outreach and supporting criminal justice reform, left before the debate escalated. Former vice presidential nominee Paul Ryan has also made efforts to reach out by discussing poverty and economic growth in various communities. Meanwhile, Democrats have taken incidents involving King to support claims that GOP stances on immigration are extreme. Alabama Rep. Mo Brooks stated in an interview that Democrats were waging a 'war on whites,' responding to questions about the GOP's standing with Hispanic voters. Brooks claimed Democrats were falsely labeling Republicans as prejudiced. California Rep. Jeff Denham was one of 11 House Republicans to oppose the deportation bill, calling the decision to bring it for a vote 'disappointing.' He argued the measure was symbolic and unlikely to pass the Senate, emphasizing the need for broad immigration reform, especially for children who have known no other country. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid had no plans to move the House bill forward, and Obama said he would veto it. Boehner wanted to keep the focus on the recent surge of Central American migrant youth, advocating for targeted legislation and resources to handle the situation. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz urged a halt to Obama's ability to defer deportations as a part of the GOP's response to border issues. Boehner allowed a vote on a stronger House conservative measure, fearing Obama might expand deferred action. Florida Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart, who voted against that measure, told CNN it plays into Democrats' strategy of using immigration as a political wedge. He and Denham criticized both Obama's unilateral actions and the risk of appearing anti-immigrant. A Republican National Committee report after the 2012 loss called on the GOP to pursue immigration reform or risk alienating Hispanic Americans. Party strategist Henry Barbour stressed the need for a positive tone and recognized the challenge of passing meaningful reform. The Wall Street Journal criticized the party for focusing on deporting children, warning it could harm the GOP's appeal among conservatives, minorities, and swing voters. Republican strategist Leslie Sanchez believes that while Hispanic support isn't based solely on immigration reform, the party's inaction and poor communication could threaten its future. Carlos Gutierrez suggested that if Republicans control the Senate, they could propose a plan combining border security with a pathway to legal status for millions, thus shifting responsibility to the President. Many Republicans interviewed by CNN warned that Democrats could use GOP divisions to further drive a wedge with Latino voters in 2016, but insisted the party should still advocate for positive reforms. Republican and Democratic campaign officials agree immigration isn't a top midterm issue, since few Republican districts have large Latino populations. Still, the 2016 race will hinge on swing states with significant Hispanic voters, such as Colorado, Nevada, Arizona, and Florida. Rep. Diaz-Balart called immigration reform the '800-pound gorilla in the room,' warning that if the GOP is seen as unwilling to tackle the issue, it could be a major obstacle with Latino voters.
translated_content: I repubblicani stanno fortemente opponendosi all’azione esecutiva prevista del presidente Barack Obama, che potrebbe permettere a milioni di lavoratori senza documenti di restare negli Stati Uniti. Nel frattempo, il dibattito sull'immigrazione mette in evidenza divisioni interne al GOP e solleva interrogativi sul fatto che il partito segua davvero i consigli per rivolgersi agli elettori ispanici. Citando l’inazione del Congresso, Obama ha affermato mercoledì scorso che non intende più aspettare che i repubblicani negozino un compromesso sull’immigrazione. 'Vi prometto che il popolo americano non vuole vedermi restare fermo senza fare nulla', ha dichiarato. Lo Speaker della Camera John Boehner ha avvertito che eventuali nuove mosse esecutive sarebbero 'un grave errore', insistendo che sia il Congresso ad agire sull’immigrazione con un approccio graduale, consentendo la partecipazione del pubblico. Sebbene Boehner abbia riconosciuto dopo le elezioni del 2012 che servisse una riforma, una proposta di legge bipartisan del Senato si è arenata alla Camera, a guida repubblicana, visto che molti parlamentari GOP di distretti sicuri temevano sfide interne e hanno preferito non portare avanti il cambiamento. Le azioni recenti di alcuni repubblicani sembrano contraddire gli sforzi per rendere il partito più inclusivo. Con il Congresso ancora diviso, Obama è deciso ad agire in autonomia. Molti leader GOP e aspiranti presidenti sostengono che un messaggio più aperto agli elettori ispanici sia fondamentale per il 2016, ma molta retorica del partito viene ancora percepita come poco accogliente dalle comunità latine. Prima della pausa di agosto, la Camera ha approvato una legge per impedire al Presidente di rinnovare o concedere sospensioni delle espulsioni a circa 600.000 giovani arrivati illegalmente negli USA da bambini. Se approvata, queste persone potrebbero rischiare l’espulsione. Il voto è stato soprattutto secondo le linee di partito e alcuni repubblicani hanno sostenuto che la misura trasmetteva il messaggio sbagliato. Carlos Gutierrez, repubblicano ed ex segretario al Commercio, ha messo in dubbio su CNN la strategia del suo partito chiedendo: 'Perché i repubblicani continuano a spararsi sui piedi?' Steve King dell’Iowa, principale promotore del disegno di legge della Camera, è stato contestato a un evento a cui partecipava anche il senatore Rand Paul. Una donna, preoccupata di essere espulsa se la legge fosse approvata, ha interrogato King. Paul, che ha lavorato per estendere la presenza GOP e sostenuto la riforma della giustizia penale, ha lasciato l’evento prima che il dibattito si scaldasse. Anche l’ex candidato vicepresidente Paul Ryan si è impegnato discutendo di povertà e crescita economica in varie comunità del Paese. Nel frattempo, i democratici hanno sfruttato episodi che coinvolgono King per rafforzare l’immagine dei repubblicani come estremi sull’immigrazione. Mo Brooks dell’Alabama ha dichiarato in un’intervista che i democratici stanno portando avanti una 'guerra contro i bianchi', rispondendo a domande sulla posizione GOP nei confronti degli ispanici. Brooks ha sostenuto che i democratici etichettano ingiustamente i repubblicani come prevenuti. Jeff Denham della California è stato uno degli 11 repubblicani alla Camera a votare contro la legge sulle espulsioni, definendo 'deludente' la decisione di metterla ai voti. Ha sostenuto che la misura fosse simbolica e improbabile da approvare al Senato, sottolineando la necessità di una riforma complessiva, specie per i ragazzi che conoscono solo gli Stati Uniti. Il leader della maggioranza al Senato, Harry Reid, non aveva in programma di portare avanti la legge della Camera e Obama ha affermato che l’avrebbe comunque bocciata. Boehner voleva mantenere il focus sull’ondata di minori migranti centroamericani, favorendo normative mirate e risorse per affrontare la situazione. Ted Cruz del Texas ha chiesto di bloccare la possibilità di Obama di sospendere le espulsioni come parte della risposta GOP ai problemi di confine. Boehner ha consentito un voto su una misura dei conservatori della Camera ancora più stringente, preoccupato che Obama potesse ampliare tali provvedimenti. Mario Diaz-Balart della Florida, che ha votato contro tale misura, ha dichiarato a CNN che così si favorisce la strategia democratica di usare l’immigrazione come tema divisivo. Sia lui che Denham hanno criticato le azioni unilaterali di Obama così come il rischio di apparire anti-immigrati. Un rapporto del Comitato nazionale repubblicano dopo la sconfitta del 2012 consigliava di affrontare la riforma dell’immigrazione, altrimenti si rischiava di alienare gli ispanici. Il stratega Henry Barbour ha sottolineato l’importanza di un tono positivo e ha riconosciuto quanto sia difficile approvare una vera riforma. Il Wall Street Journal ha criticato il partito per il suo focus sull’espulsione dei bambini, avvertendo che ciò possa danneggiare il consenso tra conservatori, minoranze e indecisi. La stratega repubblicana Leslie Sanchez sostiene che, anche se il supporto ispanico non dipende solo dalla riforma sull’immigrazione, la mancata azione e la cattiva comunicazione potrebbero danneggiare il futuro del partito. Carlos Gutierrez ha suggerito che, se i repubblicani conquistassero il Senato, potrebbero proporre un piano che unisca sicurezza dei confini e un percorso verso la legalizzazione, mettendo così la responsabilità sulla risposta del Presidente. Molti repubblicani intervistati da CNN hanno avvertito che i democratici potrebbero sfruttare le divisioni GOP per ampliare il distacco con gli elettori latini nel 2016, ma hanno insistito che il partito dovrebbe comunque proporre riforme positive. Funzionari di entrambi i partiti riconoscono che l’immigrazione non è una questione prioritaria per le elezioni di medio termine perché pochi distretti repubblicani hanno grandi comunità latine. Resta però fondamentale per il 2016 negli stati in bilico come Colorado, Nevada, Arizona e Florida. Il deputato Diaz-Balart ha definito la riforma dell’immigrazione 'il gorilla da 800 chili nella stanza', dicendo che se il GOP sarà visto come poco disposto a occuparsene, sarà un forte ostacolo con gli elettori latini.

article_content: EU-backed research is advancing comprehensive analyses of efforts to restore wild-cat populations and support vital scavenger species that help maintain ecosystem balance. A recent case in wildlife conservation illustrates the practical challenges in Europe. In spring 2023, environmentalists captured an adult male lynx in Romania's Carpathian Mountains and relocated him to Croatia's Plitvice Lakes National Park. This move aimed to boost genetic diversity among the endangered lynx populations in Croatia and Slovenia. Equipped with a telemetry collar, the lynx spent several weeks seeking a new territory. He ventured east to the Bosnian border, traveled over 100 kilometers toward Slovenia, and eventually returned to Plitvice, where he settled. Dr. Miha Krofel, a wildlife-management expert and assistant professor at the University of Ljubljana, leads the LYNXONTHEMOVE project, which is funded by the EU and runs through September 2024. The initiative examines factors influencing whether relocated lynxes remain in their release sites or move elsewhere. Despite growing success over the past two decades, recent research shows only 66% of relocated carnivores survive their first six months, and just 37% exhibit reproductive behavior. Some animals move far from targeted conservation areas. Lynxes, among Europe's most endangered species, suffered severe declines in the early 20th century due to hunting, inbreeding, habitat loss, and prey scarcity. As of recently, only 100 to 150 lynxes survived in Croatia and Slovenia. While conservation measures since the 1970s have aided recovery, populations are still declining in countries such as Austria, North Macedonia, and mountainous regions of France. Dr. Krofel collaborates with Dr. Mariano Rodríguez Recio of Rey Juan Carlos University in Spain. They use data from reintroduction efforts in Spain, Croatia, and Slovenia to analyze how environmental factors, release methods, and interactions among lynxes affect outcomes. Lynxes are elusive and mostly nocturnal, but are generally easier to reintroduce than other carnivores like wolves or bears. Success depends on release methods—either immediate release from transport or gradual acclimatization—and environmental factors such as forest cover, elevation, and human infrastructure. For instance, highways can block lynx movements, while gravel roads are used by the animals as communication channels. Interactions with other lynxes also matter: A male may avoid areas with other males, and females might do the same. The project relies on infrared cameras and telemetry collars to monitor animals and use advanced analysis to predict their behavior. The goal is to provide conservation managers with evidence-based guidance on release locations and methods. Vultures, another key group for ecosystem health, are facing challenges as biodiversity declines. Dr. Sara Asu Schroer, postdoctoral fellow at the University of Oslo, is leading the EU-funded Living with Vultures in the Sixth Extinction (LiVE) project, which explores vulture conservation from a social-sciences perspective. Schroer examines how historical, cultural, and management contexts affect vulture populations. Spain and France host over 90% of Europe’s vultures, which include griffon, bearded, cinereous, and Egyptian vultures. These scavengers play a vital ecological role by recycling nutrients and helping prevent disease spread. However, vulture populations declined due to carcass poisoning by farmers or hunters, habitat loss, and regulatory shifts like the EU ban on leaving carcasses in the wild during the mad cow crisis. Schroer’s research involves interviews with conservationists, breeders, and farmers to understand motivations and impacts. For example, the use of the drug diclofenac in India led to catastrophic vulture declines by contaminating livestock carcasses. Although European vulture populations have benefited from conservation, new threats such as veterinary drugs, power lines, and industrial development persist. Balancing wildlife needs with agricultural and regulatory practices remains complex. Schroer’s project highlights how public health policies and historical practices can shape conservation efforts, emphasizing the value of integrating social and cultural analysis with natural science to address ongoing challenges.

article_content: Indian benchmark indices S&P BSE Sensex and Nifty50 ended the week with modest gains of about 0.10%, amid mixed global signals. With a range of key domestic and global events scheduled during this holiday-shortened week, investors are anticipating market direction. On Monday, November 27, Indian equity markets will be closed due to Gurunanak Jayanti. According to Santosh Meena, Head of Research at Swastika Investmart, the markets remained largely quiet last week, with limited movement in headline indices, though some stocks saw specific activity. Favorable global cues were present, but investors are focused on the outcome of state elections and IPO-induced liquidity constraints. Meena anticipates markets may gain direction and experience increased volatility as the November F&O expiry approaches. Also, exit poll results for state elections on November 30 and India’s Q3 GDP data, both due this week, could trigger market moves. Key factors likely to affect market movement after reopening: 1) US Markets: US indices ended mixed on Friday. The Dow closed at 35,390.10 (up 117.12 points or 0.33%), S&P 500 at 4,559.34 (up 2.72 points or 0.06%), while Nasdaq finished at 14,250.80 (down 15 points or 0.11%). Indian markets will take cues from these closes and track GIFT Nifty futures, an early indicator for Nifty50. 2) Q2FY24 Earnings: Markets will react to Q2FY24 results as trading resumes Tuesday. Recently-listed Cello World announced September quarter earnings, while Siemens and ASJ Auto are scheduled to report this week. Globally, Dell Technologies will announce results. 3) Rupee vs Dollar: The rupee closed at a record low of 83.3675 against the dollar on Friday, down 0.03% from the previous 83.3425 close, pressured by weak Asian currencies and dollar demand from foreign banks. The dollar index held steady at 103.7. Anil Kumar Bhansali of Finrex Treasury Advisors LLP predicts the rupee will be range-bound (83.20–83.50) and remain under depreciation pressure, with the RBI monitoring closely. 4) Global Macros: Important US data (consumer confidence, wholesale inventories, GDP, jobless claims, ISM manufacturing PMI) will be released, along with manufacturing PMI from the UK, Eurozone consumer and economic confidence indicators, CPI, unemployment, and S&P Global PMI. China will publish industrial profits and PMI. 5) Corporate Actions: Newgen Software’s board will consider a bonus issue, CE Infosystem will discuss fundraising, BPCL’s board may declare a dividend, and Man Infraconstruction will consider fundraising. 6) Technical Factors: Nifty faces resistance at 19,800–19,850. A breakout may lead to 19,990–20,150; immediate support lies at 19,700, and a key demand zone at 19,600–19,550. Bank Nifty, while underperforming, shows recovery from its 200-DMA of 43,300. The 50-DMA at 44,000 acts as a hurdle, with critical resistance at 44,400. 7) FII/DII Action: Foreign and domestic institutional investors will be vital in Monday’s market performance. On Friday, FIIs were net buyers of Rs 2,625.21 crore, and DIIs bought Rs 134.46 crore. V K Vijayakumar of Geojit Financial Services notes declining US inflation and bond yields have led to reduced FII selling, and expects renewed FPI interest in banking stocks, possibly driving a large-cap rally. 8) Gold: Gold saw over 1% weekly gains due to the Fed’s suggestive dovish stance. December gold futures closed at Rs 61,370, up Rs 298 or 0.49% over Thursday’s close. Silver futures on December closed at Rs 75,584 per kg, up Rs 1,019 or 1.37%. On Comex, gold closed at $2,003.70 (down $10.90 or 0.55%), and silver at $24.38 (up $0.69 or 2.92%). 9) Crude Oil: Crude oil prices declined this week ahead of the delayed OPEC+ meeting on November 30. WTI crude settled at $75.18 (down $1.92 or 2.49%), while Brent futures closed at $80.58 (down $1.19 or 1.46%). MCX December crude oil ended at Rs 6,338, down Rs 36 or 0.56%. 10) Bond Yields: Indian government bond yields rose after weak demand in the weekly auction. The benchmark 7.26% 2033 bond closed at 7.2704% from 7.2561% previously, rising five basis points for the week. New Delhi raised Rs 300 billion in bonds, but weaker demand for the 14-year paper pushed yields up. Ajay Manglunia of JM Financial noted that yields are tracking US rates and oil prices, and this trend will continue until the RBI’s policy announcement in December. article_content: In east London, British architect Marcus Lee relaxes outside his family's home as streams of unfamiliar faces explore inside, snapping photos and checking out every room—even his underwear drawer. Lee isn’t bothered; he’s one of many residents opening their private homes, offices, and public buildings for London’s annual Open House weekend. Now in its 20th year, Open House gives the public rare access to architecturally significant buildings across the city, most of which are usually off-limits. Victoria Thornton, the event’s founding director, says it’s a great way for people to connect with London’s diverse architectural landscape. For some, it’s also just a fun way to satisfy their curiosity about their neighbors’ lives. Lee’s house, which has won several architectural awards, is made from Siberian larch and uses advanced rainwater collection with sustainable materials. Graphic design student Laura Coren loves how open, bright, and stylish it feels, noting her interest in the art and books inside as much as the home’s design. A short distance away in Hackney, Sutton House offers a glimpse into London’s past. Built in 1535, it’s one of the city’s oldest brick Tudor homes and still boasts original features like a large stone fireplace and detailed wood panels. National Trust custodian Robyn Finne points out that the house has served many roles over the centuries—including home, church, school, and squat—mirroring the city’s constant evolution. Some homeowners see Open House as a chance to share eco-friendly practices. James Wright, who renovated his Victorian home, leads tours focused on his sustainable choices, such as installing solar water heaters and upgrading insulation to preserve classic sash windows. Afterward, he’s peppered with questions about topics from chemical-free paints to easy-clean walls. Throughout the city, visitors carrying their green guidebooks board buses and trains between sites. Becky Stevens, en route to Norman Foster’s 'Gherkin,' sums it up: 'Even though we’re allowed in, it feels a bit mischievous—like a special secret for locals, while tourists stick to places like Big Ben.'

Giunto al suo ventesimo anno, Open House offre al pubblico accesso raro a edifici architettonicamente importanti della città, la maggior parte normalmente chiusa ai visitatori. Victoria Thornton, direttrice fondatrice dell’evento, sostiene che sia un ottimo modo per connettersi con la varietà architettonica di Londra. Per altri è anche solo l’occasione perfetta per soddisfare la propria curiosità sulle case degli altri. La casa di Lee, premiata con diversi riconoscimenti architettonici, è costruita con larice siberiano e utilizza sistemi avanzati di raccolta dell’acqua piovana e materiali sostenibili. article_content:
The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation announced Wednesday a donation of $50 million to help combat the Ebola outbreak in West Africa. Over 2,200 people have died in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, where the outbreak is most severe. Cases have also been reported in Nigeria and Senegal. According to the foundation, the funds will enable international aid organizations and national governments to purchase urgently needed supplies and expand emergency operations in affected countries.

The foundation will also collaborate with partners in the public and private sectors to accelerate the development of therapies, vaccines, and diagnostics for treating patients and preventing further transmission of Ebola. Last week, the first human trial of an experimental Ebola vaccine began at the National Institutes of Health in the United States. 

This is considered the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history. On Monday, the World Health Organization (WHO) stated that the virus's rapid spread in Liberia shows no sign of slowing, describing the situation as a "dire emergency with unprecedented levels of human suffering." The WHO reported that taxis crowded with families fearful of Ebola travel throughout Liberia's capital looking for treatment, but no hospital beds are available. As soon as a new treatment center opens, it immediately fills beyond capacity, according to the United Nations group.

To help relieve pressure on West Africa's overstretched health care system, the United States announced Tuesday it will send an additional $10 million, adding to the $100 million already provided to support the fight against Ebola. USAID also pledged $75 million more, which will fund transportation and support for 100 additional health care workers combating the epidemic.

The WHO and various nonprofit agencies working on the ground have repeatedly called for the international community to send more trained personnel. USAID funding has already provided 130,000 sets of personal protective equipment, 50,000 hygiene kits, and 1,000 new hospital beds. Additionally, USAID has launched a website where trained nurses, physician assistants, and doctors can sign up to volunteer.

On Sunday, President Barack Obama emphasized that addressing the Ebola outbreak should be a national security priority. In an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," Obama said the U.S. military could help by setting up isolation units and providing security for medical staff. He warned that if efforts are not intensified and the disease spreads beyond Africa, there's a risk the virus could mutate, potentially making it easier to transmit and posing a greater threat globally.

CNN's Betsy Klein contributed to this story.

Secondo la fondazione, i fondi consentiranno alle organizzazioni di aiuto internazionali e ai governi locali di acquistare forniture urgenti e potenziare le operazioni di emergenza nei paesi colpiti.

USAID ha inoltre promesso altri 75 milioni di dollari, che finanzieranno il trasporto e il sostegno per altri 100 operatori sanitari impiegati contro l'epidemia.

L'OMS e molte organizzazioni non profit attive sul campo hanno ripetutamente chiesto alla comunità internazionale di inviare più personale qualificato. I fondi di USAID hanno già permesso la fornitura di 130.000 kit di dispositivi di protezione individuale, 50.000 kit igienici e 1.000 nuovi letti ospedalieri. Inoltre, USAID ha lanciato un sito web dove infermieri, assistenti medici e medici qualificati possono iscriversi per dare il proprio contributo.

Domenica, il presidente Barack Obama ha sottolineato che la lotta all'epidemia di Ebola deve diventare una priorità per la sicurezza nazionale. In un'intervista per "Meet the Press" della NBC, Obama ha dichiarato che l'esercito americano potrebbe aiutare allestendo unità di isolamento e assicurando la sicurezza del personale sanitario. Ha avvertito che, se non si agisce subito e la malattia dovesse diffondersi oltre i confini africani, esiste il rischio che il virus muti, rendendosi più facilmente trasmissibile e diventando una minaccia più seria a livello globale.

article_content: Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf, who was scheduled to appear in court on Thursday for his trial, has been hospitalized after feeling unwell, his lawyer told CNN. According to his lawyer, Ahmad Raza Kasuri, Musharraf was admitted to a hospital based on medical advice. The court subsequently postponed his trial until Monday. Asiya Ishaq, a supporter and leader of the All Pakistan Muslim League, stated that Musharraf had experienced chest discomfort since Wednesday evening and was not feeling well. She said, when asked about the possibility of him seeking treatment in Dubai, that 'Musharraf will not leave Pakistan.' Ishaq also mentioned that, to her knowledge, 'Musharraf has three blocked arteries and is currently undergoing an angiography,' a medical imaging procedure for arteries. Atiqa Odho, a Pakistani actor and former leader of the APML—a party founded by Musharraf in 2010—expressed her support on Thursday. 'I pray for President Musharraf's health and long life,' she said. 'It is painful to see a great and brave man heartbroken, having been let down by people who once claimed to support him.' If convicted of treason, Musharraf could face life imprisonment or the death penalty. Prosecutors allege that he violated Pakistan's constitution by declaring emergency military rule in 2007. Musharraf led Pakistan from 1999 to 2008. After leaving office in 2008, he went into exile, but returned to Pakistan last year intending to participate in national elections. His plans were disrupted as he became involved in several court cases related to his time in office. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif accused Musharraf of illegally suspending the constitution in November 2007. At that time, Musharraf declared a state of emergency, suspended the constitution, replaced the chief judge, and imposed a blackout on independent TV channels. Musharraf stated that his actions were intended to stabilize the country and confront rising Islamist extremism. However, the measures drew strong criticism from the United States and democracy activists, and many Pakistanis called for his resignation. Facing pressure, Musharraf eventually lifted the state of emergency and promised elections. He resigned in August 2008 as the governing coalition moved toward impeachment. A spokeswoman for Musharraf said in November that he is willing to address all the charges against him. 'Gen. Musharraf has full faith in the judiciary and trusts the legal system to clear his name,' said Aasia Ishaque to CNN. 'He is a man of his word and will let the court decide his fate.' Reporting by CNN's Jethro Mullen.

article_content: SpaceX's Starship faced another setback during its second space launch attempt. Early Saturday, the rocket lifted off from Boca Chica, Texas, with all 33 Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster performing as expected. Starship successfully detached from its booster, an improvement over the first flight, but the booster exploded on its descent. Starship continued climbing for nearly six minutes before SpaceX lost communication. The reason for this loss and where Starship was at the time remain unknown. According to SpaceX engineer John Insprucker, the automated safety system might have triggered late in the flight while the rocket was over the Gulf of Mexico. Standing at nearly 400 feet tall and boasting about 16 million pounds of thrust thanks to the Super Heavy stage, Starship could be the biggest and most powerful launch vehicle to reach space if it surpassed the 62-mile mark. Starship is a cornerstone in Elon Musk's vision, including deep-space exploration, launching Starlink satellites, rapid international travel, and potential Mars settlement. Its full reusability is designed to cut launch costs and enable repeated missions. In addition to Musk's ambitions, NASA has selected Starship for future lunar landings, and entrepreneur Yusaku Maezawa plans to take a private moon trip aboard. Starship’s explosive tests reflect SpaceX’s rapid, iterative development philosophy: launch, learn, and improve. After the initial launch in April ended in failure and caused significant launchpad damage, SpaceX enhanced the ship’s separation system, reinforced the pad, and installed a water deluge setup for better heat management. Despite months of upgrades, the most recent flight revealed new setbacks, with no clear timeline on the next attempt.

La Starship ha continuato a salire per quasi sei minuti prima che SpaceX perdesse ogni comunicazione. Le cause della perdita di contatto e la posizione esatta della Starship restano sconosciute. La Starship è al centro della visione di Elon Musk: esplorazione dello spazio profondo, messa in orbita dei satelliti Starlink, viaggi rapidissimi sulla Terra e in futuro la colonizzazione di Marte. Nonostante mesi di aggiornamenti, l’ultimo volo ha mostrato nuove sfide e non si sa ancora quando avverrà il prossimo lancio.

article_content: U.S. officials have urged Pakistan to strengthen oversight of a fertilizer frequently used to build homemade bombs in Afghanistan. Senator Robert Casey from Pennsylvania highlighted that Pakistani authorities have yet to act on their commitment made in August to enhance control measures. He specified that steps like limiting fertilizer access, marking it with tracking dyes, and stopping its unlawful movement at the Afghan border are crucial. According to the U.S. military, 84% of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) discovered in Afghanistan are produced using fertilizer sourced from Pakistan. These devices have caused more than 400 American military deaths in the past two years, making them the number one threat to U.S. forces in the area. A Pakistani official, speaking anonymously, responded by noting that their government is working on the issue but emphasized the immense challenge of monitoring vast quantities of legally manufactured fertilizer. Calcium ammonium nitrate, the fertilizer in question, is approved for farming in Pakistan but has been prohibited in Afghanistan since 2009. Pakistani manufacturer PakArab describes the product as useful for all types of crops, soil, and climate conditions. Despite its agricultural benefits, law enforcement has intercepted large shipments—Afghan officials stopped a convoy carrying enough fertilizer to make over 2,000 bombs last year. Specialist Seth Jones from the RAND Corporation explained that strict border controls are hindered by the high volume of cross-border traffic and the region’s porous geography. Smugglers continue moving bomb-making ingredients via key routes including the Helmand River Valley and Khyber Pass. This call for stricter controls comes as diplomatic tensions rise between the U.S. and Pakistan. Recently, Admiral Mike Mullen accused Pakistan’s intelligence agency of supporting the Haqqani network, a charge Pakistani officials deny. Senator Casey stands firm, stating he will persist in urging for stronger safeguards while American troops remain at risk. He stressed that inaction is indefensible given the tools and expertise available to address the problem.

article_content: The National Boundary Commission (NBC) has partnered with seven Northern States in Nigeria that share borders with the Niger Republic to address security challenges and foster economic cooperation and integration across Africa. This was announced during a one-day workshop held in Sokoto for the creation of a platform for Local Border Authorities along the Nigeria-Niger international boundary. NBC's Director General, Adamu Adaji, revealed that the Federal Government is keen on transforming borders into opportunities for collaboration rather than separation. The workshop, themed 'Transforming borders from barriers of separation to bridges of cooperation and integration,' aimed to encourage the proactive use of human resources for peacebuilding and improving standards of living in border communities. Adaji urged participants to champion peace and highlighted that the platform would be extended to all border areas of Nigeria. The new platform is designed to facilitate implementation of decisions made by the Border Governors Forum, strengthen engagement between local authorities, traditional institutions, and neighboring countries. Nigeria's seven Northern States have twenty local governments bordering the Niger Republic. Sokoto State’s Deputy Governor and Chairman of its Boundary Committee, Eng. Idris Muhammad Gobir, praised the Federal Government's commitment to fostering cooperation among key stakeholders and building enduring relationships. He emphasized that the platform will help tackle security issues, such as banditry in border communities, and create joint development projects to enhance living conditions. Junaid Abdullahi, Executive Secretary of the Border Communities Development Agency (represented by Sadiq Abdullahi), expressed the agency’s dedication to partnering with stakeholders and implementing robust border management policies under its Strategic Action Plan. The event was attended by Deputy Governors from Kebbi, Katsina, Jigawa, Zamfara (represented), Borno, Yobe (represented), and a representative of the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III.

Adaji ha invitato i partecipanti a essere promotori di pace, sottolineando che la piattaforma sarà estesa a tutte le aree di confine della Nigeria. A new instructional video has been released by the Alabama Department of Homeland Security, providing guidance on how to survive a mass shooting. The six-minute video, originally created by the Houston Police Department and adapted for use in Alabama, was published on November 5. It uses dramatized scenes and a suspenseful soundtrack to demonstrate what to do if caught in an active shooter situation at work.

The video advises following three steps: run, hide, or, as a last resort, fight. The footage depicts an armed attacker entering an office building, with employees reacting in different ways—some escaping, some hiding, and some preparing to defend themselves using available office items like a fire extinguisher, chair, coffee pot, or belt.

A narrator reminds viewers: 'You have to be prepared for the worst,' emphasizing the need for a plan if ever involved in an active shooter event. The video highlights the importance of quick decision-making: attempt to flee if possible, hide if escape is not an option, and, only if necessary, confront the attacker. While viewers are encouraged to help others, the narrator warns not to let indecision slow you down in an emergency.

The video concludes with the surviving employees gathered outside by a fire truck, and a disclaimer appears, noting that each individual must use their own discretion during such events. The release comes amid several deadly shootings across the U.S., including the recent tragedy at Sandy Hook Elementary School on December 14, 2012, where 20 children and six staff members lost their lives. The video has generated significant discussion online about gun control and personal safety.

Le immagini mostrano un aggressore armato che entra in un edificio di uffici, con i dipendenti che reagiscono in modi diversi: alcuni fuggono, altri si nascondono e altri si preparano a difendersi usando oggetti disponibili come un estintore, una sedia, una caffettiera o una cintura.

Un narratore ricorda agli spettatori: "Devi essere preparato al peggio", sottolineando l’importanza di avere un piano in caso ci si trovi coinvolti in una sparatoria. Il video evidenzia la rapidità decisionale: tentare di fuggire se possibile, nascondersi se non si può scappare e, solo se strettamente necessario, affrontare l’aggressore. Sebbene si incoraggi ad aiutare gli altri, il narratore avverte di non lasciarsi rallentare dall’indecisione in caso di emergenza.

Il video si conclude con i dipendenti sopravvissuti raccolti fuori vicino a un camion dei pompieri, seguito da un avviso che specifica come ciascuno debba usare il proprio giudizio in tali eventi. L’uscita del video arriva dopo diverse sparatorie negli Stati Uniti, tra cui la recente tragedia alla scuola elementare Sandy Hook del 14 dicembre 2012, in cui persero la vita 20 bambini e sei membri dello staff. Il video ha suscitato ampie discussioni online sul controllo delle armi e la sicurezza personale.

Fears that the much-anticipated Comet ISON — predicted to be up to 15 times brighter than the Moon — had broken up have been alleviated by new images from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. The space agency confirmed that the comet, an icy object making a risky journey around the Sun, remains intact and is on course to pass through our inner solar system from November through January.

It is hoped that Comet ISON will deliver a spectacular display for observers in the Northern Hemisphere. A Hubble colour composite image, taken on October 9 when the comet was inside Mars' orbit and about 177 million miles from Earth, shows its nucleus still intact with a greenish-blue coma created by gas and a tail formed from dust pushed outward by sunlight. The comet could become visible even in daylight if it survives its close encounter with the Sun.

Although some astronomers worried that the comet’s icy nucleus might break apart as it approaches the Sun — coming within about 730,000 miles of its surface on November 28 — the Hubble images from October show no evidence of such disintegration. The 'head' around the nucleus appears symmetric and smooth, which experts say would not be the case if fragments were breaking away.

Previously, in July, astronomers saw a polar jet of dust, but this feature is no longer visible, possibly indicating changing activity. Early predictions from scientists, including Ignacio Ferrin of the University of Antioquia in Colombia, warned that Comet ISON might not survive, but current observations are more optimistic.

Discovered in September 2012 by two amateur Russian astronomers, Comet ISON (named after the International Scientific Optical Network) likely originates in the Oort Cloud, a distant region of icy bodies surrounding the Sun. At the time of discovery, it was more than 584 million miles from the Sun.

As ISON approaches, it is expected to accelerate rapidly, reaching speeds over 400,000 miles per hour as it passes near the Sun. Its closest approach to Earth will be on December 26, at a distance of around 39.9 million miles. While there’s still a chance the comet could disintegrate during its close solar pass, if it survives, scientists aim to study its composition by observing which gases vaporize as it heats up. Temperatures may reach 4,900°F (2,700°C), hot enough to melt lead, and the Sun’s gravity could still tear the comet apart.

Early data suggest ISON’s nucleus could be up to 1.2 miles (nearly 3 kilometers) across, potentially large enough to avoid complete evaporation. If its density and rotation are typical, skywatchers may be able to spot the comet without special equipment from mid-November into mid-January.

Astronomers worldwide, coordinated via channels such as NBC News and using telescopes like Gemini North’s Multi-Object Spectrograph, are observing ISON’s journey. If the comet survives this encounter, it may not return to the inner solar system for thousands or even millions of years.

Le paure che la tanto attesa Cometa ISON — che si prevedeva potesse essere fino a 15 volte più luminosa della Luna — si fosse disintegrata sono state dissipate da nuove immagini scattate dal Telescopio Spaziale Hubble della NASA. L’agenzia spaziale ha confermato che la cometa, un corpo ghiacciato che sta compiendo un viaggio rischioso intorno al Sole, è ancora intatta e si sta avvicinando al nostro sistema solare interno da novembre fino a gennaio.

Si spera che la Cometa ISON offrirà uno spettacolo spettacolare per gli osservatori dell’emisfero nord. Un’immagine a colori composita, scattata da Hubble il 9 ottobre mentre la cometa era all’interno dell’orbita di Marte e a circa 285 milioni di chilometri dalla Terra, mostra il suo nucleo ancora intatto con una chioma verde-azzurra formata dai gas e una coda creata dalla polvere spinta dalla luce solare. La cometa potrebbe essere visibile persino di giorno, se riuscirà a sopravvivere al suo incontro ravvicinato con il Sole.

Sebbene alcuni astronomi temessero che il nucleo ghiacciato della cometa potesse frantumarsi avvicinandosi al Sole — passando a circa 1,2 milioni di chilometri dalla sua superficie il 28 novembre — le immagini di Hubble di ottobre non mostrano segni di disintegrazione. La "testa" attorno al nucleo appare simmetrica e liscia: secondo gli esperti, non sarebbe così se si stessero staccando frammenti.

A luglio, gli astronomi avevano osservato un getto polare di polvere, ma questo fenomeno ora non è più visibile, probabilmente segnale di un’attività cambiata. Le previsioni iniziali di alcuni scienziati, tra cui Ignacio Ferrin dell’Università di Antioquia in Colombia, sostenevano che la Cometa ISON potesse non sopravvivere, ma le osservazioni attuali sono più ottimistiche.

Scoperta nel settembre 2012 da due astronomi dilettanti russi, la Cometa ISON (dal nome dell’International Scientific Optical Network) proviene probabilmente dalla Nube di Oort, una regione remota ricca di corpi ghiacciati che circonda il Sole. Al momento della scoperta, si trovava a oltre 940 milioni di chilometri dal Sole.

Avvicinandosi, ISON accelererà fino a oltre 640.000 km/h durante il passaggio vicino al Sole. Il punto più vicino alla Terra sarà il 26 dicembre, a circa 64 milioni di chilometri di distanza. C’è ancora la possibilità che la cometa si disintegri durante il suo passaggio ravvicinato, ma se sopravvive, gli scienziati potranno studiarne la composizione osservando quali gas si libereranno scaldandosi. Le temperature potrebbero raggiungere i 2.700°C (4.900°F), sufficiente a fondere il piombo, e la gravità del Sole potrebbe ancora distruggere la cometa.

I primi dati stimano che il nucleo di ISON sia grande fino a 2 chilometri, forse abbastanza per non evaporare del tutto. Se densità e rotazione sono tipiche, la cometa potrebbe essere visibile a occhio nudo da metà novembre a metà gennaio.

Astronomi da tutto il mondo, grazie anche a fonti come NBC News e strumenti come lo spettrografo del telescopio Gemini North, stanno seguendo il percorso di ISON. Se la cometa sopravvive, potrebbe non tornare nell’interno del sistema solare per migliaia o persino milioni di anni.

James Cleverly has taken charge of the Home Office, promising to lead the department in his own way. As Home Secretary, he is responsible for policing, immigration, and national security—some of the most significant areas in government.

Asked whether he wished to move away from predecessor Suella Braverman’s rhetoric, Cleverly said, "I intend to do this job in the way that I feel best protects the British people and our interests."

Cleverly faces an overflowing in-tray. At the forefront is the ongoing debate about pro-Palestinian protests. Downing Street reportedly wants him to review police powers immediately, making it easier to ban marches and prosecute those glorifying terrorism. However, this will not be simple. Lowering the threshold for banning protests would likely trigger legal challenges, given that the right to freedom of assembly and association is protected by the European Convention on Human Rights and UK law. Banning a protest march is only lawful if it is in the interest of national security or to prevent serious public disorder.

Policing leaders maintain that decisions on arrests during protests are operational matters. There is also a risk that aggressive tactics, such as using snatch squads to arrest protesters for hate crimes, could actually increase the likelihood of public disorder.

Within days of taking office, Cleverly must deal with the Supreme Court’s imminent decision on the government’s plan to send some asylum seekers to Rwanda. This ruling, expected Wednesday morning, could present an immediate crisis if the Home Office loses. Even if the government wins, legal challenges by individuals facing removal to Rwanda are expected to continue.

Cleverly echoed the Prime Minister’s focus, stating the government wants to deliver on its promises to stop small boat crossings, protect the public, and ensure people feel secure. Over 26,000 migrants have crossed the Channel this year—a significant drop from last year—but ministers believe the threat of being moved to East Africa is the key deterrent to smuggling gangs.

The Home Secretary also inherits an overwhelmed asylum system, with 175,000 people waiting for initial decisions and tens of thousands still housed in hotels at a daily cost of about £8 million.

One immediate dilemma is a Home Office plan to relocate 1,700 single male migrants to a former RAF base at Wethersfield near Braintree in Essex—Cleverly’s own constituency. He has previously voiced opposition to using this site.

Cleverly’s style is markedly different from Braverman’s. At the Foreign Office, he was considered measured and diplomatic, a job he relished. When speculation arose about him moving to Defence Secretary in a previous reshuffle, he joked that if removed, "you will see nail marks on the parquet floor in my office."

Now, Cleverly must adapt his approach to reflect the government’s determination to appear tough on crime and punishment in the run-up to the next election.

Ora Cleverly dovrà adattare il suo stile per riflettere la determinazione del governo nel mostrarsi severo contro la criminalità e risoluto in tema di punizioni, in vista delle prossime elezioni.

article_content: The Swarajya Sanghatana, advocating for Maratha reservation, has warned Maharashtra minister and OBC leader Chhagan Bhujbal that they may disrupt his movements in the state if he continues to oppose the Maratha quota and activist Manoj Jarange-Patil. Dhananjay Jadhav, head of the Swarajya Sanghatana’s Pune unit, stated the group would not remain silent if Bhujbal persists with his criticisms. On Monday in Pune, tensions flared at the VVIP Circuit House when Swarajya Sanghatana members and Bhujbal's supporters nearly clashed before police intervention. The group stated they intended to urge Bhujbal to stop making remarks that, in their view, divide the Maratha and OBC communities and impede reservation efforts. Jadhav noted that Bhujbal’s speeches at rallies in Jalna and Hingoli seemed designed to widen the gap between the two groups. At a Jalna rally, Bhujbal accused Jarange-Patil of fleeing during a police crackdown at a protest for Maratha reservation. In Hingoli, Bhujbal called for ending the Justice Sandeep Shinde committee and pausing the issuance of Kunbi certificates to Marathas, insisting that Marathas should receive separate reservations and not be included in the OBC category. Jadhav emphasized that the Swarajya Sanghatana upholds Sambhajiraje Chhatrapati’s principle of communal harmony. He said their confrontation with Bhujbal was a warning, and if divisive statements continued, the group would act to restrict his free movement in Maharashtra. Jadhav asserted that Jarange-Patil had not targeted the OBC community, but only OBC leaders hindering Maratha reservation. He added that Jarange-Patil praised those within the OBC community supporting the Maratha cause. Jadhav accused Bhujbal of deliberately fueling division and suggested he should learn from Jarange-Patil’s approach. On Monday, Jarange-Patil withdrew a remark about Marathas working under 'undeserving people' after it was perceived as disrespectful to OBCs in Maharashtra, clarifying his focus is on supporting his own community.

article_content: Catwoman, also known as Selina Kyle, has served as both adversary and ally to Batman across decades, transforming from a classic villain into an antihero with her own title. A new dimension of her character is highlighted in 'Catwoman' #39, where Selina Kyle’s bisexuality is confirmed. In this latest issue written by Genevieve Valentine, Selina is shown kissing Eiko Hasigawa, who has recently taken on the identity of Catwoman, while Selina leads as a crime boss. Valentine explains in her blog that Selina’s romantic interests are not a recent development but rather a confirmation: 'She’s flirted around it—often quite literally—for years now.' For readers fond of Selina’s dynamic with Batman, Valentine assures that this aspect of her story is still present, commenting, 'Selina’s longstanding connection to Batman has not been forgotten; that’s not how bisexuality (or humanity) works.' She further describes how Eiko offers both a moral challenge and support to Selina, allowing space to explore trust amidst adversity: 'Eiko has offered a moral challenge—and we know Selina loves a challenge—but also unexpectedly given Selina trust and support at a time when it’s in short supply. Selina is a complex figure, drawn to complicated people. In one sense, it’s that simple—even if it’s never quite so simple.' The series has previously featured LGBTQ+ representation, including Holly Robinson, for which Catwoman won a GLAAD media award in 2004, and the introduction of Batwoman as a lesbian character in 2006 (with her series now nearing its end). Following the revelation of Catwoman’s sexuality, fans were quick to respond and share their thoughts on Twitter.

Valentine spiega nel suo blog che gli interessi romantici di Selina non sono una novità, ma una conferma: 'Ci ha girato intorno—spesso letteralmente—per anni.' La serie in passato ha già mostrato rappresentazione LGBTQ+: con Holly Robinson, ruolo grazie al quale Catwoman ha ottenuto un GLAAD Media Award nel 2004, e con l’introduzione di Batwoman come personaggio lesbica nel 2006 (la cui serie sta ora per finire). Officials representing Venezuela's government and opposition have inked an agreement to set the stage for jointly recognized presidential elections in the second half of 2024. Under the terms, international observers will be invited to oversee the vote—a response to criticisms that the previous 2018 election lacked fairness and transparency. 

The deal, signed in Barbados following nearly a year of stalled dialogue, marks a notable advance, though analysts caution that it falls short of addressing core opposition demands such as the release of political prisoners and lifting of bans on certain opposition figures. 

The US, EU, Canada, and UK have welcomed the agreement, describing it as a critical step towards inclusive dialogue and democratic restoration in Venezuela. These nations, however, continue to push for more, calling for the freedom of all political detainees, the independence of both the electoral process and judiciary, press freedom, and protection of human and political rights.

Spanning twelve points, the agreement promises equitable media access and safe campaigning for all candidates, and pledges to refresh voter registries inside and outside Venezuela—ensuring that millions of Venezuelans abroad can cast their ballots.

Disputes remain over candidate eligibility. The agreement says registration is open to all constitutionally qualified candidates, yet interpretations vary. Opposition leader Gerardo Blyde suggests this framework could allow previously banned candidates to participate, while government representative Jorge Rodríguez insists bans imposed by the comptroller-general are still in force. This affects several high-profile opposition members, notably María Corina Machado, a leading candidate for the opposition, who remains determined to run regardless of her current ban, arguing that pressure will force its eventual removal if she is selected.

Though the government has not announced its nominee, President Maduro is broadly anticipated to run again. The administration hopes that the agreement will spur eased US sanctions—imposed following the contested 2018 election—as part of wider efforts to relieve Venezuela’s severe economic crisis, which has pushed more than seven million Venezuelans to emigrate, many heading to the US. With Venezuela home to the world’s largest proven oil reserves, sanction relief stands to benefit both Venezuela and the United States economically.

L'accordo prevede la presenza di osservatori internazionali che supervisioneranno il voto, rispondendo alle critiche sulle elezioni del 2018, ritenute da molti né trasparenti né eque.

Siglato alle Barbados dopo quasi un anno di stallo nelle trattative, l'accordo rappresenta un notevole passo avanti. Tuttavia, gli analisti fanno notare che non affronta questioni fondamentali sollevate dall’opposizione, come la liberazione dei prigionieri politici o la revoca dei divieti che colpiscono alcuni esponenti dell’opposizione.

Stati Uniti, Unione Europea, Canada e Regno Unito hanno espresso apprezzamento, definendo l’accordo un importante passo verso un dialogo inclusivo e la restaurazione della democrazia in Venezuela. Tuttavia, continuano a sollecitare ulteriori avanzamenti, tra cui la liberazione incondizionata dei detenuti politici, l’indipendenza dei processi elettorali e giudiziari, la libertà di stampa e il rispetto dei diritti umani e politici.

Restano però divergenze sull’ammissibilità dei candidati: l’accordo prevede che possano iscriversi tutti coloro che rispettano i requisiti costituzionali, ma le interpretazioni sono diverse. Il negoziatore dell’opposizione, Gerardo Blyde, ritiene che ciò possa consentire il ritorno dei candidati esclusi, mentre il rappresentante governativo Jorge Rodríguez ribadisce che le interdizioni imposte dal controllore generale rimarranno valide. Romania and Hungary have evacuated a total of 460 of their citizens from Israel as violence in the region escalates. According to the Romanian Foreign Ministry, 245 Romanian nationals were flown out on four planes—two operated by state-owned TAROM and two by private airlines. Among the evacuees were also two groups of pilgrims.

Meanwhile, the Hungarian government airlifted 215 citizens from Tel Aviv using two Hungarian Air Force Airbus A319 military aircraft. The planes, which serve as standby aircraft for government use, landed at Budapest Airport on Monday morning. This mass evacuation follows the large-scale attack on Israel by Hamas militants. Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó shared updates about the operation on social media.

The evacuations occurred amidst ongoing conflict in the region, as governments act to protect their citizens abroad.

At I.S. 318 Eugenio Maria De Hostos in New York, 12-year-old Preston Cabral usually eats meat at home but looks forward to Meatless Mondays and Vegan Fridays at school. Recently, he enjoyed a lunch of chips, tangerines, and a meatless bean chili. These themed days have even led his family to eat more vegetarian meals, a shift praised by health and environmental experts as beneficial for both people and the planet.

Initiatives like these tackle the challenge of encouraging reduced meat consumption. According to an AP-NORC poll, most Americans continue to eat meat regularly, with 64% consuming chicken or turkey and 43% eating beef several times a week. Experts warn that current meat-eating habits, particularly in wealthier nations, contribute to health issues such as obesity and heart disease, and significantly impact the environment. In fact, U.S. adults average 100 grams of protein a day—mostly from meat—double the recommended amount. Statistics from the United Nations show Americans consume over 328 pounds of meat per person annually, including substantial quantities of poultry, beef, pork, and seafood.

Meat production has a sizeable environmental footprint. The UN estimates livestock accounts for at least 14.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions and is a leading source of methane, a potent contributor to climate change. Studies from Oxford University reveal vegan diets create only 30% of the environmental impact of high-meat diets, while even moderate meat reduction makes a notable difference. "You don’t have to go full vegan or vegetarian to see benefits," notes researcher Keren Papier.

Young people may be particularly receptive to updating their diets due to growing climate awareness, but experts like Dr. Martin Bloem from Johns Hopkins highlight that behavioral change is slow. Meat remains integral to American culture and identity, sustained by advertising and notions around health, according to nutrition researcher Julia Wolfson. She references famous campaigns like "Beef: It’s What’s for Dinner" to illustrate this cultural tie.

This deep connection complicates efforts to cut down on meat, as many people resist learning about the negative sides of their habits—a phenomenon called the 'meat paradox.' The AP-NORC poll found that Americans value taste, price, and nutrition more highly than environmental or animal welfare when choosing their food.

Even so, researchers have shown that interventions like menu changes, showing pictures of source animals, and making vegetarian meals the default option can substantially lower meat consumption. For instance, making non-meat meals the standard choice at conferences in a study led to vegetarian selections rising from 2% to nearly 90%.

Policy measures are being discussed overseas—such as a proposed meat tax in the Netherlands and an upcoming ban on industrial meat advertising in Haarlem. However, similar steps are not popular in the U.S.; around 70% of surveyed adults oppose higher meat taxes, and nearly half object to meat ad bans in public spaces.

Meanwhile, meat-free menu initiatives are growing. Meatless Monday programs in schools worldwide are raising awareness and inspiring small but meaningful changes. At Preston’s school, Fridays attract the highest number of students for lunch—vegan meals now outpace even hamburgers and pizza in popularity, reports school cook ambassador Ricardo Morales.

The AP-NORC survey included 1,247 U.S. adults, with a sampling error margin of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. This coverage is part of The Associated Press’s work, which is supported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute’s Science and Educational Media Group, though the AP maintains full editorial independence.
